summary: Dr. Anju Kambadur leads Bloomberg's AI Engineering group of 400+ researchers across London, New York, Princeton, and Toronto. Bloomberg invested 15-16 years in AI, built BloombergGPT in 2022, then pivoted to building on open-source and open-weight models. He distinguishes tools from agents using the cognitive architectures for language agents spectrum. Bloomberg processes 400 billion ticks of structured data daily, over a billion unstructured messages, and millions of documents with 40 years of history. Non-negotiable product principles include precision, comprehensiveness, speed, throughput, availability, data protection, and transparency. The first product discussed is earnings call transcript summarization (2023), where out-of-the-box LLM performance was poor, requiring remediation workflows, circuit breakers, CI/CD, and monitoring. The architecture is semi-agentic with mandatory coded guardrails. Kambadur addresses two scaling challenges. First, building robust agents: LLM compositions multiply errors, unlike well-documented deterministic software. A 2009 news sentiment product shows even controlled systems had out-of-band communication. With agentic architectures, release cycles shift to daily improvements, and downstream consumers make independent changes, so model version changes require notification. A US CPI query example demonstrates compounding errors: a single missed character returned monthly instead of quarterly data, nearly impossible to catch when only an answer is shown. The mindset shift is to assume upstream fragility and build own safety checks rather than requiring handshake sign-offs. Second, rethinking org architecture: traditional ML had a software factorization reflected in org structure (Conway's law). Early on, collapse to vertical teams for fast iteration and code/data/model sharing. As products mature, move to horizontal teams for optimization, cost reduction, testability, and transparency. Guardrails are a horizontal concern—no team should independently solve rejecting financial advice inputs. The current research agent architecture factors out question understanding and answer generation as separate agents, with non-optional guardrails called at multiple points, building on years of data infrastructure evolution from sparse to dense to hybrid indices.

sections.title: Introduction and Bloomberg's AI Journey
sections.summary: Kambadur introduces Bloomberg's AI history, from building BloombergGPT in 2022 and publishing in 2023, to pivoting toward building on top of open-source and open-weight models as the community progressed.

sections.title: AI Engineering Organization and Tool vs Agent Definitions
sections.summary: Describes the AI Engineering group: 400 people, 50 teams across four cities. Introduces vocabulary distinguishing tools (left side of cognitive architectures spectrum) from agents (autonomous, with memory, can evolve).

sections.title: Bloomberg's Scale and Research Analyst Archetype
sections.summary: Bloomberg handles 400 billion ticks of structured data daily, a billion+ unstructured messages, millions of documents, with 40 years of history. Focuses on the research analyst archetype and lists non-negotiable product principles.

sections.title: First Product: Earnings Call Summarization
sections.summary: Describes a 2023 product generating summaries of quarterly earnings call transcripts. Out-of-the-box LLM performance was poor, requiring remediation workflows, circuit breakers, CI/CD, and monitoring because published summaries have outsized error impact.

sections.title: Semi-Agentic Architecture and Scaling Introduction
sections.summary: Current architecture is semi-agentic with mandatory coded guardrails such as not offering financial advice. Kambadur introduces two aspects of scaling and focuses on the first.

sections.title: Scaling Aspect 1: Robust Software and Error Multiplication
sections.summary: Contrasts well-documented software like matrix-matrix product with stochastic ML model APIs. LLM-based agent compositions multiply errors causing fragility. A 2009 news sentiment product example shows even controlled systems had out-of-band communication.

sections.title: Downstream Communication and Compounding Errors
sections.summary: With agentic architectures, release cycles shift to daily improvements, requiring downstream notification of model version changes. A US CPI query example shows a single missed character returned monthly instead of quarterly data—nearly impossible to catch when only an answer is shown. The mindset shift is to assume upstream fragility, build own safety checks, and avoid requiring handshake sign-offs from every downstream consumer before releasing.

sections.title: Scaling Aspect 2: Org Architecture and Team Structure
sections.summary: Traditional ML had a software factorization reflected in org structure (Conway's law). Early on, collapse to vertical teams for fast iteration and sharing of code, data, and models. As products mature, move to horizontal teams for optimization, cost reduction, testability, and transparency. Guardrails are a horizontal concern—not every team should independently solve rejecting financial advice inputs. Timing of creating horizontals and breaking out monolithic agents matters.

sections.title: Research Agent Architecture Today
sections.summary: The current research agent takes in user world and session context, deeply understands the question, and figures out what information is needed—factorized as its own agent reflected in the org structure. Answer generation is separately factored out with rigor around well-formed answers. The architecture is semi-agentic with non-optional guardrails called at multiple points. Infrastructure builds on years of data evolution from sparse to dense to hybrid indices.

limitations: Out-of-the-box LLM performance on precision, accuracy, and factuality was poor
